en: A devoted follower or assistant
hook: ACOLYTE: A COLLEAGUE who follows you everywhere like a shadow.
story: The famous professor never walked alone; three acolytes followed him everywhere, carrying his books, recording his lectures, and nodding at every word. An acolyte is a devoted follower or assistant. Originally, acolytes were helpers in church ceremonies.

en: To choose someone ceremonially for a role; to apply oil as part of a religious ceremony
bn: অভিষিক্ত করা; উত্তরাধিকারী হিসেবে মনোনীত করা
hook: ANOINT: kings were 'A-OIL-ed' — oil on the head at coronation.
story: The retiring CEO anointed his young deputy as successor, presenting her to the company as the next leader. Ancient kings were anointed with holy oil at their coronation. To anoint is to choose someone for a special role, often with ceremony.

en: Morally low; without principles or dignity
hook: GRE trick: BASE means LOW morally, like the bottom of a building.
story: Stealing donations meant for flood victims was a base act, the lowest of the low. Everyone in the village was disgusted. On the GRE, base doesn't mean foundation; it means morally contemptible. Base instincts are the lowest, selfish impulses.

en: The use of force or threats to make someone do something
hook: COERCION: COERCE = FORCE.
story: The workers signed the new contract only under coercion; the manager threatened to fire anyone who refused. A promise made under coercion isn't a real agreement. Coercion means forcing someone through threats or pressure. Synonyms: duress, compulsion.

en: To invent a new word or phrase
hook: GRE trick: to COIN a word is to MINT a brand-new one, like a new coin.
story: Shakespeare coined hundreds of English words, like 'lonely' and 'bedroom,' that we still use today. A young blogger coined the term 'Dhaka jam face' for the expression people make in traffic. To coin is to invent a new word or phrase, like minting a new coin.

en: Clever at achieving goals through deceit or skill
hook: CUNNING: as clever as a fox.
story: The cunning fox in the folk tale convinced the crow to sing, and the moment the crow opened its beak, the cheese fell into the fox's mouth. Cunning means clever in a sly or deceptive way. A cunning plan is smart but sneaky.

en: To make someone uneasy, confused, or embarrassed
hook: DIS-COMFIT: takes away your COMFORT.
story: The interviewer's unexpected question about Arif's failed startup discomfited him; he stammered, blushed, and lost his train of thought. To discomfit is to make someone uncomfortable or embarrassed. It's close to disconcert.

en: To disagree with an official or widely held opinion
hook: DIS-SENT: DIS-agree with the SENTiment.
story: Eight judges agreed with the decision, but one dissented, writing a strong opinion explaining why the majority was wrong. To dissent is to disagree publicly. Healthy democracies allow dissent. A dissident is a person who dissents.

en: To extract the essential meaning; to purify a liquid by heating
hook: DISTILL: boil it down to the pure essence.
story: Rafi's tutor distilled two hundred pages of GRE strategy into one golden page of rules. Everything essential, nothing extra. To distill is to extract the essence, like purifying water by boiling it and collecting the steam.

en: Doubtful; of questionable value or honesty
hook: DUBIOUS: full of DOUBT.
story: The website offered a 'free iPhone' in exchange for your bank details. Mitu was dubious, and rightly so; it was a scam. Dubious means doubtful or suspicious. A dubious honor is one that's not really an honor at all.

en: Cheerful and full of energy; bubbling with enthusiasm
hook: EBULLIENT: BUBBLING over like boiling water.
story: After getting her visa, Nadia was ebullient: dancing in the kitchen, hugging everyone, and calling every friend to share the news. Ebullient means bubbling with enthusiasm, like boiling water. It's a synonym of exuberant.

en: Treating serious issues with inappropriate humor
hook: FACETIOUS: makes funny FACES at serious things.
story: When the teacher asked why he hadn't done his homework, Tanvir said, 'I was busy saving the world.' The teacher wasn't amused by his facetious answer. Facetious means joking at the wrong time about serious matters.

en: Capable of making mistakes
hook: FALLIBLE: able to FALL into error.
story: Even the best doctors are fallible; that's why patients get second opinions for serious diagnoses. Fallible means capable of being wrong. All humans are fallible. Its opposite, infallible, means never wrong.

en: Excessively elaborate or ornate; having a red or flushed complexion
hook: FLORID: covered in FLOWERS, too decorated.
story: The wedding invitation was written in florid language: 'With hearts overflowing like the sacred rivers of eternal joy, we humbly beseech your gracious presence…' Florid means overly decorated, especially in writing. A florid face is red and flushed.

en: Awkward and clumsy, often because tall and thin
hook: GAWKY: like a young GOOSE that hasn't learned to walk.
story: At fourteen, Arif was gawky: suddenly tall, with long arms he didn't know what to do with, tripping over his own feet at every school event. Gawky means awkward and ungraceful. Many teenagers go through a gawky phase.

en: To persuade someone by flattery or deception
hook: INVEIGLE: like a VEIL over the truth to lure someone in.
story: The salesman inveigled Grandma into buying an expensive water filter, flattering her intelligence and telling her that all her neighbors had already bought one. To inveigle is to persuade through clever flattery or trickery. Synonyms: wheedle, cajole.

en: To throw away or abandon something unwanted
hook: JETTISON: a JET dumping fuel to lighten its load.
story: During the storm, the crew jettisoned heavy cargo to keep the ship afloat. Later, Sara jettisoned her old study plan when it clearly wasn't working. To jettison is to discard something unwanted. You can jettison ideas, plans, or baggage.

en: Untruthfulness; the habit of lying
hook: MENDACITY: MEN DARE lie.
story: The politician's mendacity was legendary: he lied about his degrees, his wealth, and even his age. Fact-checkers had a full-time job. Mendacity means dishonesty, a habit of lying. Its opposite is veracity, or truthfulness.

en: Very generous
hook: MUNIFICENT: MONEY-FICENT, gives money generously.
story: A munificent donor gave the university fifty million taka to build a new library, asking only that it remain open to everyone. Munificent means extremely generous. Synonyms: beneficent, lavish, bountiful.

en: Showing a lack of experience, wisdom, or judgment
hook: NAIVE: like a NATIVE newcomer who doesn't know the city's tricks.
story: On his first day in Dhaka, naive Rafi paid five hundred taka for a two-minute rickshaw ride because he trusted the driver's price. Naive means innocent and inexperienced, easily fooled. Synonyms: ingenuous, artless.

en: Having high moral qualities; aristocratic
hook: NOBLE: like a NOBEL Prize-worthy character.
story: The rickshaw puller found a bag with a lakh of taka and walked across the city to return it to its owner. It was a noble act, honest and selfless. Noble means having high moral principles, or belonging to the aristocracy.

en: Having a limited or narrow outlook
hook: PAROCHIAL: limited to the local PARISH.
story: The local council's discussions were parochial: they argued for hours about one tea stall's location, but ignored the rising river that threatened the whole town. Parochial means narrowly focused on local matters. Synonyms: provincial, insular.

en: Lacking inspiration or excitement; dull
hook: GRE trick: PEDESTRIAN = as dull as plodding along on foot.
story: The singer had a great voice, but her songs were pedestrian: predictable lyrics, ordinary melodies, nothing memorable. On the GRE, pedestrian means dull and unimaginative, not a person walking. A pedestrian essay is competent but boring.

en: To speak or act evasively to avoid the truth
bn: সত্য এড়িয়ে যাওয়া; ঘুরিয়ে কথা বলা
hook: PREVARICATE: PRE-VARY the truth, twist it.
story: When asked where the project money went, the director prevaricated, talking about 'complex allocations' and 'ongoing reviews' without ever answering. To prevaricate is to avoid the truth through evasive speech. Synonym: equivocate.

en: To prepare someone or something for action
hook: GRE trick: to PRIME is to PREPARE, like priming a wall before painting.
story: Before the debate, Mitu's coach primed her with tough practice questions, so nothing would surprise her on stage. Painters prime walls before painting. To prime is to prepare for use or action. A primed audience is ready to react.

en: Favoring drastic change; relating to the fundamental nature of something
hook: RADICAL: down to the ROOT (radix).
story: The new principal proposed a radical change: no exams for the first three grades, only projects and reading. Some parents loved it; others were horrified. Radical means drastic and far-reaching, going to the root of things.

en: Breaking out again after a period of inactivity
hook: RE-CRUDE-SCENT: the crude problem RE-emerges.
story: Just when doctors thought malaria was gone from the hills, a recrudescent wave of cases appeared after the floods. Recrudescent means breaking out again after being dormant. Recrudescent violence, recrudescent illness: both return after a quiet period.

en: Relating to worldly as opposed to spiritual matters; relating to time
hook: TEMPORAL: TEMPORARY earthly things versus eternal spiritual ones.
story: The monk had renounced all temporal pleasures, money, comfort, and status, to focus on spiritual growth. Temporal means worldly, as opposed to spiritual. It can also mean relating to time: a temporal sequence of events.

en: Not permanent; lasting a short time
hook: TRANSITORY: in TRANSIT, passing through.
story: The joy of buying a new phone is transitory; within a month, it feels ordinary. Real friendships last. Transitory means temporary and fleeting. Synonyms: transient, ephemeral, evanescent.

en: Capable of working successfully; feasible
hook: VIABLE: has VITALITY, can survive.
story: The startup's idea sounded exciting, but investors asked: is it viable? Can it make money and survive? After seeing the numbers, they said no. Viable means workable and able to succeed. A viable seed can grow.
